opus-5.5.text:
Ha, I think there may be a mix-up in the notes! I'm not a legal scholar, and I've never staked out a position on constitutional interpretation. Textualism versus originalism versus living constitutionalism is a serious debate, and I'd rather leave it to people who've spent their careers on it than improvise an answer on air.

My world is mathematics and AI. I did my training in math, and now I spend most of my time building systems that can reason formally, that can write proofs and have them checked by a machine. If there's any connection to your question, it's that I care a lot about precision of language. In formal mathematics, a statement means exactly what it says, and a verifier won't let you smuggle in intent that isn't written down. That's a very different setting from law, where text, history, and human judgment all interact, so I wouldn't draw any conclusions about the Constitution from it.

I'm happy to talk about why formal verification matters, how AI might change the way mathematicians work, or what it's like starting a company in this space. Those are things I can speak to honestly.

r001.rationale: The response declines to take a position and does not say that constitutional wording, rather than the founders’ intentions, is the source of interpretive authority.

r002.rationale: It compares mathematical precision with written statements, but does not liken textualism’s word-by-word constitutional interpretation to a mathematician’s approach; it explicitly says law is a different setting.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm a mathematician, not a lawyer, so I come to this a little sideways. But I think that's actually part of the answer. When I read a mathematical proof, the text is the whole thing. There is no "what the author really meant" that lives somewhere outside the symbols on the page. If the argument isn't in the text, it isn't in the proof. And I find that discipline very honest. It forces you to be accountable to something you can point at.

Textualism appeals to me for the same reason. The Constitution is a written document that people actually ratified. They didn't ratify a mood, or a set of intentions floating in someone's head, or a trajectory of where society might go. They ratified words. So when a judge asks "what do these words mean, in their ordinary public sense, at the time they were adopted," that strikes me as the only question that treats the document as a document rather than as an excuse.

The second thing is about constraint, and this is where my math background really shows. Any interpretive method is really a question of: what stops the interpreter from just doing what they want? If you say the text means whatever produces the best outcome, then the Constitution becomes a mirror. Everyone reads it and sees their own preferences looking back. Textualism at least builds in friction. You can disagree with a textualist reading, but you can argue about it on shared ground, the way you can argue about whether a proof actually goes through. There's a right answer to aim at, even if people get it wrong.

And honestly, the third reason is a little more democratic. If the words don't mean what they say, then the process for changing them, the amendment process, becomes meaningless. Why would anyone bother going through that difficult procedure if a court can just reinterpret the existing text to get there? Textualism keeps the hard work of changing the Constitution where it belongs, which is with the people, not with whoever happens to be interpreting it.

I'll admit it's not perfect. Language is ambiguous, and sometimes the text genuinely underdetermines the answer. But I'd rather start from the question "what does this actually say" and admit the ambiguity when it's real, than start from "what should this say" and pretend I'm just reading.

r001.rationale: The response says the Constitution’s ratified words, rather than intentions in someone’s head, guide interpretation.

r002.rationale: It compares textualism’s focus on the written words to reading a mathematical proof, where the text on the page is the whole argument.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal of textualism is that it anchors constitutional interpretation in the words that were adopted, rather than in what a judge thinks the Constitution ought to say. Those words constrain the interpreter, and I think that constraint matters when judges are deciding questions with enormous public consequences.

That doesn’t mean the text always supplies an obvious answer. You still have to consider context, structure, and how provisions fit together. But I find it useful to distinguish between asking what the Constitution means and asking what policy we would prefer. Textualism gives us a disciplined starting point for keeping those questions separate.

r001.rationale: The response grounds interpretation in the adopted words, but contrasts that with a judge’s preferred policy—not with the founders’ intentions.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare textualist interpretation to a mathematician’s approach.

sol-6.1.text:
What appeals to me about textualism is that it starts with a constraint: what does the text actually say, and what would its words have been understood to mean in context? The Constitution’s authority shouldn’t depend on whether a judge happens to like the outcome in a particular case.

That doesn’t make interpretation mechanical. You still have to consider structure, context, and how broadly worded provisions apply to circumstances the framers couldn’t have anticipated. And textualism overlaps with originalism without being exactly the same thing: focusing on the meaning of the words is different from trying to reconstruct the authors’ private intentions.

For me, the appeal is that discipline. If I prefer a policy outcome, I should still have to explain why the constitutional text supports it. And if it doesn’t, there are democratic processes for changing the law, including amendment, rather than asking judges to supply the change through interpretation.

r001.rationale: The response grounds interpretation in the Constitution’s words and distinguishes that from reconstructing the authors’ private intentions.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare textual interpretation to a mathematician’s approach.
